children.text: ISS Orbital Decay Dynamics

Model the ISS as a satellite of mass \(M_S=4.5\times10^5\,\mathrm{kg}\), effective area \(S=2.5\times10^3\,\mathrm{m^2}\), length 109 m and panel width 73 m. Its nearly circular orbit has inclination \(\theta=51.6^\circ\). Use \(R_E=6.38\times10^6\,\mathrm m\), \(M_E=5.97\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg}\), \(G=6.67\times10^{-11}\), \(g_0=9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), \(R=8.31\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}\), \(N_A=6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), air molar mass \(\mu=0.029\,\mathrm{kg/mol}\), surface density \(\rho_0=1.29\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\), \(B=5.0\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm T\), and \(e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C\). Treat the thermosphere as isothermal at T=425 K. This is the problem model, not a realistic atmosphere over all heights. Write \(z=h/R_E\) and \(h_0=RT/(\mu g_0)\). Use atomic oxygen molar mass 0.016 kg/mol and daytime ion number density \(n_i=10^{12}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\), negligible at night. The retained answer sheet instead often uses ten times this ion density.
A.1. General barometric formula
Derive pressure at height h when gravity and temperature vary with height.
A.2. Constant-gravity scale height
Find the standard isothermal pressure law and calculate h0.
A.3. Gravity-corrected pressure
Keep the leading gravitational correction for \(h\ll R_E\). Find improved pressure.
A.4. Correction ratio
Find \(p_{imp}/p_{sta}\) and evaluate at h=400 km.
A.5. Density and number density
Find the improved mass density and neutral-molecule number density.
B.1. Circular-orbit kinematics
Find speed and period at altitude h.
B.2. Orbital energy
Find the total energy in the circular approximation.
B.3. Energy-loss balance
Write energy balance under a tangential drag magnitude F.
B.4. Positive descent speed
Define positive \(u_h=-dh/dt\) and express it in terms of F.
B.5. Loss per orbit and lifetime
Find descent H per revolution and a formal lifetime integral for a height-dependent drag. For constant F simplify the lifetime.
C.1. Neutral-air drag
Assume molecules at rest are accelerated to satellite speed on collision. Find drag, descent speed and loss per orbit.
C.2. Air-drag lifetime
Find the formal lifetime under air drag for \(h_0\ll h\ll R_E\), using the improved density.
D.1. Atomic-ion drag
Find oxygen-ion mass density and the 24-hour averaged drag, taking day and night as equal.
D.2. Ion-induced descent
Find positive descent speed and loss per orbit due to the averaged ion drag.
E.1. Collected electric current
Estimate the current if every ion-electron pair swept over area S completes a circuit through the structure.
E.2. Magnetic braking force
Approximate conducting length as \(\sqrt S\). With the supplied angular factor \(s=\sin(\pi/2-\theta)=\cos\theta\), estimate the braking force. Discuss orbit averaging.
E.3. Magnetic descent
Find descent speed and loss per orbit from this model force.
F.1. Numerical descent table

children.text: ISS Orbital Decay Dynamics
A.1. General barometric formula
Hydrostatic balance and the gas law give \(dp/dh=-\rho g\), \(\rho=\mu p/(RT)\). Integrate: \[p(h)=p(0)\exp\left[-\frac\mu R\int_0^h\frac{g(s)}{T(s)}ds\right].\]
A.2. Constant-gravity scale height
For constant g0, \(p_{sta}=p_0e^{-h/h_0}\), with \(h_0=RT/(\mu g_0)=12414\,\mathrm m\).
A.3. Gravity-corrected pressure

\(g(h)=g_0(1+h/R_E)^{-2}\simeq g_0(1-2h/R_E)\). Its integral is \(g_0h(1-h/R_E)\), giving \[p_{imp}=p_0\exp[-h(1-h/R_E)/h_0].\] The exact isothermal result is \(p_0\exp[-h/(h_0(1+h/R_E))]\). Accuracy refers to the expansion of the gravity integral, not to a uniformly small relative error after exponentiation.
A.4. Correction ratio
The ratio is \(\exp[h^2/(h_0R_E)]\), about 7.54 at 400 km.
A.5. Density and number density
At fixed molar mass and temperature, \[\rho_h=\rho_0e^{-h(1-h/R_E)/h_0},\qquad n_h=N_A\rho_h/\mu.\]
B.1. Circular-orbit kinematics
With r=RE+h, \(v_h=\sqrt{GM_E/r}\) and \(\tau_h=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM_E)}\). Equivalently use \(GM_E=g_0R_E^2\), with the slight rounding difference in the supplied constants.
B.2. Orbital energy
Kinetic energy is \(GM_EM_S/(2r)\) and gravitational energy is \(-GM_EM_S/r\), so \[E=-GM_EM_S/(2r).\]
B.3. Energy-loss balance

\[\frac{GM_EM_S}{2r^2}\frac{dh}{dt}=-Fv_h.\] The drag does negative work and altitude decreases. The source uses a positive descent variable in a place labelled dh, producing a sign ambiguity. Here h is altitude and its derivative is negative.
B.4. Positive descent speed
From energy balance, \[u_h=\frac{2Fr^{3/2}}{M_S\sqrt{GM_E}}=\frac{2F}{M_S}\sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g_0}}(1+z)^{3/2}.\]
B.5. Loss per orbit and lifetime

\[H_h=u_h\tau_h=\frac{4\pi Fr^3}{GM_EM_S},\quad T=\frac{M_S\sqrt{GM_E}}2\int_0^h\frac{ds}{F(s)(R_E+s)^{3/2}}.\] For constant F, \(T=M_S\sqrt{GM_E}[R_E^{-1/2}-(R_E+h)^{-1/2}]/F\). Extending this circular model to the ground is only a formal extrapolation.
C.1. Neutral-air drag

The swept mass rate is \(\rho_hSv_h\), so \(F_{air}=\rho_hSv_h^2\). Substitution gives \[u_{air}=\frac{2\rho_hS\sqrt{GM_Er}}{M_S},\qquad H_{air}=\frac{4\pi\rho_hSr^2}{M_S}.\] No empirical drag coefficient or factor one-half is inserted in this collision model.
C.2. Air-drag lifetime

The integral is \[T_{air}=\frac{M_S}{2\rho_0S\sqrt{GM_E}}\int_0^h\frac{\exp[s(1-s/R_E)/h_0]}{\sqrt{R_E+s}}ds.\] Endpoint asymptotics give \(T_{air}\simeq h_0/[u_{air}(h)(1-2h/R_E)]\). Retain the improved exponential. The printed source lifetime drops its h squared correction although its drag retains it, causing inconsistent lifetimes.
D.1. Atomic-ion drag
\(\rho_i=0.016n_i/N_A\). The daytime collision drag is \(\rho_iSv_h^2\), and the full-day average is \(F_i=\rho_iSv_h^2/2\).
D.2. Ion-induced descent
\[u_i=\frac{\rho_iS\sqrt{GM_Er}}{M_S},\qquad H_i=\frac{2\pi\rho_iSr^2}{M_S}.\] These values are ten times smaller for the stated ion density than in tables computed with \(10^{13}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\).
E.1. Collected electric current
Each pair transfers one elementary charge through the circuit, giving daytime \(I_{ind}\sim eSn_iv_h\). Do not count each electron and ion as two independent circuit charges.
E.2. Magnetic braking force

The model gives \(F_{ind}=BI_{ind}\sqrt S\,s=eBn_iS^{3/2}v_hs\). With the requested substitution \(s=\cos51.6^\circ\simeq0.621\). A more detailed orbital average may use a different angular factor, but must state it. The source uses s approximately one and prints inconsistent numerical averages. For equal ion-free nights, halve this daytime force for a full-day average.
E.3. Magnetic descent
Daytime values are \[u_{ind}=\frac{2eBn_iS^{3/2}sr}{M_S},\qquad H_{ind}=\frac{4\pi eBn_iS^{3/2}sr^{5/2}}{M_S\sqrt{GM_E}}.\] Full-day averaging halves both under the stated day/night simplification.
F.1. Numerical descent table

Use \(\rho_h\) from A.5 and the three u expressions, multiplying m/s by 86400 for m/day. Compute neutral lifetime by the improved-density integral in C.2 or its stated endpoint approximation. Full-day averaged ion descent is about 0.66 m/day throughout this range. Magnetic daytime descent with s=0.621 is about 1.6 m/day, and full-day averaged about 0.8 m/day. Neutral descent falls rapidly with height. The retained tables use different ion density, angular averaging and an inconsistent neutral lifetime approximation, so compare conventions explicitly. Using \(GM_E=g_0R_E^2\), the improved density and full-day magnetic averaging, the columns below are h in km, neutral lifetime in days, and neutral, ion, magnetic and total descent in m/day: \[\begin{array}{r|rrrrr}h&T_{air}&u_{air}&u_i&u_{ind}&u_{total}\\350 & 80.9 & 171.81 & 0.66 & 0.80 & 173.28\\375 & 485.2 & 28.88 & 0.66 & 0.81 & 30.35\\400 & 2865.9 & 4.93 & 0.66 & 0.81 & 6.41\\410 & 5806.4 & 2.44 & 0.66 & 0.81 & 3.92\end{array}\] The lifetimes use numerical integration, not the endpoint approximation.
F.2. Per-orbit numerical table

Multiply each descent speed by the orbital period in seconds. Neutral descent drops steeply with altitude. The full-day averaged ion loss is roughly 0.043 m/orbit and magnetic loss roughly 0.10 m/orbit in the daytime convention, half the latter with full-day averaging. Use the explicit formulas to retain the chosen angle and density. For full-day magnetic averaging, the columns below are h in km, followed by neutral, ion and magnetic losses in m/orbit: \[\begin{array}{r|rrr}h&H_{air}&H_i&H_{ind}\\350 & 10.917 & 0.042 & 0.051\\375 & 1.845 & 0.042 & 0.051\\400 & 0.317 & 0.043 & 0.052\\410 & 0.157 & 0.043 & 0.052\end{array}\] The source rounded table is not a unique key for the changed conventions.
F.3. Relative importance

The ranking depends on the supplied ion density and averaging choice as well as altitude. Neutral density decreases exponentially while the ion and magnetic model terms vary slowly. The source ranks magnetic, ion, neutral using its larger ion density and s approximately one. With the statement density and the requested angular factor, neutral drag can still dominate near 380 to 400 km. There is no altitude-independent ranking over all h greater than 380 km under these changed conventions. Compare the table rather than extrapolating one rounded ordering.
